front: Try now, 1 minute: close your eyes. Imagine a tiger closing in, with no way out. Hear its feet and its breath. Then ask: how much does it weigh?
back: Notice what happens to the fear when wonder comes in. Hudson says wonder and fear are hard to hold together.
extra: Use it for lesser fears, such as being fired. Not for real danger.

front: For which fears does Hudson suggest the tiger exercise, and for which not?
back: For lesser fears, such as being fired. Not for real danger.

front: How do you "walk through the outcome" of a fear?
back: Picture the steps before, during and after it, again and again. Feel what it would bring.

front: What is the "say the scary truth" practice?
back: Ask what scary thing is true for you right now. Then say it out loud.

front: What does Hudson suggest the body does with fear, and with whom?
back: Let it shake and let sounds out. He recommends doing this with others.

front: How can you tell that fear is really moving?
back: The story changes, and relief follows.

front: If you feel the fear but the story stays the same, what may be going on?
back: You may be feeling it only to get rid of it.
extra: This links to the Golden Algorithm: welcoming a feeling only to make it leave is still resisting it.

front: In Hudson's Fear Triangle, feeling stuck means you are in which role?
back: The victim.

front: In Hudson's Fear Triangle, feeling angry and alone means you are in which role?
back: The bully.

front: In Hudson's Fear Triangle, feeling obligated means you are in which role?
back: The savior.

text: What are you {{c1::defending}}? What is the {{c2::you that you are defending}}? What makes you think it {{c3::can be destroyed}}?

front: Try, the next time anxiety comes: go to its most intense part. Ask what the really scary thing is. Stay 5 seconds.
back: Then go on with your day. Notice how the anxiety feels after those 5 seconds.

front: How long does Hudson say to stay at the most intense part of anxiety?
back: Five seconds. Then go on with your day.
extra: First ask what the really scary thing is.

front: What odd question does Hudson suggest asking about anxiety?
back: "How is my anxiety right now?" Then feel the answer.
extra: The odd wording keeps the head out of it.

text: Ask what you are scared {{c1::will happen}}. Then ask what you would have to {{c2::feel}} if it did.

front: What is the "I'm excited" experiment?
back: Jump up and down and say "I'm excited" 10 times in a row.

front: His guide says fear can be excitement without what?
back: Breath. So breathe.

front: What question finds the step that anxiety points to?
back: What one step would settle this?

front: Besides a step to take, what else does Hudson check for in anxiety?
back: Anger, grief or fear under it. And whether you are refusing to feel calm.

text: For {{c1::one week}}, write down {{c2::each thing that goes right}}. Write {{c3::the first anxious thought that comes after it}}. Look for {{c4::themes}}.
Each time shame comes: {{c1::stop}}. {{c2::Invite}} it. {{c3::Love}} it. Tell it that {{c4::it can come back at any time}}. Move when you are ready.
extra: Hudson calls this the fastest way through shame.

front: Try now, 1 minute: recall a small moment of shame. Stop. Invite it. Love it. Tell it that it can come back at any time.
back: Notice what changes when you stop pushing it away. Move on when you are ready.

front: What question looks under shame?
back: What would I have to feel if I could not feel ashamed right now? Then feel that.

front: The question "what would I feel if I could not feel ashamed?" is also the tool for which problem?
back: Regret that replays.

front: You keep doing something you hate. Where does Hudson say to look?
back: For the shame around the habit.

front: How do you "find the want" in shame?
back: Describe what you truly want, and feel the desire inside the shame.

front: How do you find a double bind?
back: Name a want. Ask if you also want its opposite, and if neither feels okay.

front: What does Hudson call the best route through shame?
back: Saying the shameful thing to people who care for you.

front: In a fight where shame passes back and forth, how many people have to stop?
back: Only one.

front: To drop the hot potato, what do you say, face to face?
back: That nothing in you wants the other person to feel ashamed or bad right now.
extra: Then notice any wish to shame them.

text: Sit or stand with your {{c1::back straight}}. Say {{c2::what happened}} and {{c3::which part you are responsible for}}. Say that {{c4::it is not how you want to be}}, and that you apologise.

front: Which word do you avoid in an upright apology?
back: "You".

front: In an upright apology, what do you not try to do?
back: Change how the other person feels.

front: Try: pick one small thing you did. Sit upright and say the apology out loud: what happened, your part, that it is not how you want to be. Leave out "you".
back: Notice how it feels to own your part without trying to change their feelings.

front: What is the "twenty apologies" exercise?
back: List the times you were passive-aggressive. Make about 20 upright apologies.

front: How much does Hudson say twenty apologies cut passive aggression, and how sure is it?
back: By a third or so. It is his guess. He did not measure it.

front: For a bad habit, what daily apology does Hudson suggest?
back: Apologise to yourself each day for the harm the habit does.

front: What question uses guilt as a door back to your wants?
back: If I could not feel guilty, what else would I notice or want?

front: You feel guilty or "dirty" after a talk. What does Hudson say this probably means?
back: You were trying to control the talk.

front: What can you say plainly to refuse a guilt trip?
back: That you are not interested in being guilt-tripped.

front: Instead of refusing a guilt trip outright, what can you ask?
back: Name the guilt trip, and ask what makes them do it right now.

front: Which part of Hudson's method does research dispute most?
back: His anger work. The essay says to read the evidence section before you start.

front: Held-in anger: where can it turn when it does not go out?
back: On yourself. You attack yourself.
extra: One of his four signs that anger is held in.

front: Held-in anger: how can it leak sideways?
back: As sarcasm, lateness or guilt trips.
extra: One of his four signs that anger is held in.

front: Held-in anger: what pattern does it show over time?
back: It builds and then blows up.
extra: One of his four signs that anger is held in.

front: Held-in anger: what can it collapse into?
back: Feeling stuck and low.
extra: One of his four signs that anger is held in.

front: May you aim your anger at a person?
back: Never without their permission.

front: What must anger release never do to bodies or things?
back: Never hurt yourself or others. Never break things.

front: In Hudson's view, what is it when you use anger to scare or control someone?
back: Manipulation.

text:
1. {{c1::Find a safe place}}.
2. {{c2::Set a time}}.
3. {{c3::Keep part of you outside it}}.
4. {{c4::Use the body and voice}}.
5. {{c5::Tell your body it is safe}}.
6. {{c6::Check that it is done}}.

front: Anger release, step 1: what counts as a safe place?
back: A pillow, a car, a beach, or a room with loud music.

front: Anger release, step 2: how long do you tell yourself you will listen to the anger?
back: 15 to 20 minutes. He suggests 40 for people who are low.

front: Anger release, step 3: how do you keep part of you outside the anger?
back: Treat it as a role you perform well, like an actor who plays rage.

front: Anger release, step 3: if you tend to shut down, what do you do first?
back: Lean into the story a little.

front: Anger release, step 4: how do you use the body and voice?
back: Yell, open the chest and make sounds. Heavy music can help.
extra: Keep his rules: aim it at no one without permission, hurt no one, break nothing.

front: Anger release, step 5: what do you tell your body?
back: That it is safe: no one is attacking you, and you are not hurting anyone.

front: Anger release, step 6: what does real completion bring?
back: Relief and clarity about you, not a verdict on them.

front: Clean anger test: what is it not trying to do to anyone?
back: Control, target or blame them.

front: Clean anger test: how does it leave you?
back: Clearer and more open.

front: Why may you feel more anger for a while after you stop holding it in?
back: As when a kink comes out of a hose: what was held back comes through. Expect it.

front: During anger release you start to collapse. What does Hudson suggest?
back: Use your will. Repeat a short line such as "No. I won't collapse."

front: During anger release you leave your body or lose track of time. What do you do?
back: Return to the role, or to the timed listening.

front: Anger keeps coming back fast. Where does Hudson say to look?
back: For fear, hurt or grief under it.

front: What is "commute anger"?
back: Get angry alone in the car each night, with no one there.
extra: He reports change in two or three weeks for one client.

front: What do you tell your family in "announce and leave"?
back: That you are angry, that you do not want to take it out on them, and that you will drive for 20 minutes.

front: Anger: what do you do before the talk with the other person?
back: Release the anger first.
key: Which comes first: releasing the anger, or the talk with the other person?

context: Anger: ask what it cares about
text: What do I {{c1::care about}} here? What {{c2::line was crossed}}? What {{c3::clarity}} is it looking for?

front: Try, alone in a safe place, aimed at no one: set a timer for 15 minutes. Let the anger out through body and voice, as a role you play well.
back: At the end, notice: do you have relief and clarity about you, or a verdict on them?
extra: Do not hurt yourself or others, and do not break things. The essay says to read the evidence section first.

front: What does "mourn before you decide" ask you to do?
back: Assume the outcome you dread, such as a marriage ending. Mourn it fully. Then decide what to do.

front: Try, 5 minutes: pick a decision you fear. Assume the dreaded outcome has happened, and let yourself mourn it.
back: Notice whether the decision looks different once the grief has had room.

front: How much crying does Hudson say some built-up feeling needs?
back: About 10 minutes.

front: Hudson's story: how did a friend of his give grief a place?
back: He drove a long road each week and wailed and raged in the car.
extra: The idea is easy to borrow: give grief a set time and place.

front: Hudson's story: what did he do when he could not cry for years?
back: He went off alone and faked crying for about three months, until real crying came.

front: When you practise crying, how does Hudson say to watch it?
back: As you would watch the Grand Canyon.

front: What does guest Alexa Anderson do to move through grief?
back: She spends about a minute on each feeling in turn, in the body.
extra: The feelings: sadness, fear, anger, shock, denial, acceptance and gratitude.

text: After a breakup, grieve {{c1::the person}}, {{c2::the patterns}} and {{c3::the future you pictured}}.

context: Grief: four phases of a breakup
text:
1. You mourn {{c1::the person}}.
2. You mourn {{c2::what taught you to chase or earn love}}.
3. {{c3::The body still cries, with little story left}}.
4. You {{c4::miss the heartbreak a little}}.
extra: They come in waves.

context: Grief: four phases of a breakup
front: What does Hudson say speeds up the phases of a breakup?
back: Sound and movement.
extra: He says most people do not get through all four phases without them.

front: What does Hudson say each heartbreak does to you?
back: It widens your capacity to love.

front: In Hudson's view, are people who shut down after heartbreak broken by the pain?
back: No. They are avoiding the pain.

front: Where does Hudson say to look for helplessness?
back: Where you control the most. Helplessness is often under it.

front: How do you play out the worst case?
back: Name one thing you cannot let go of. Picture the worst in detail. Do Emotional Inquiry on what comes.

front: Why also picture the thing going perfectly?
back: The good version can be the scarier one.

text: Letting go cannot be {{c1::forced}}. Feel how much {{c2::holding on hurts}}, as with a hot pan, and letting go follows.

front: Try now, 30 seconds: press your palms together and try to pull your little fingers apart. Notice the trying. Then feel its opposite.
back: Notice what trying feels like in the body, and what its opposite feels like.

context: Helplessness: how do I want to be?
front: How do you answer the question "how do I want to be right now?"
back: By being that way, not in words.

context: Helplessness: how do I want to be?
front: How often, and for how long, does Hudson suggest asking "how do I want to be right now?"
back: 20 times a day for a couple of weeks. He says this makes a clear difference.

front: For deep release, such as shaking or old pain, who should be with you?
back: A grounded person: someone who is not in fear.

front: What does Hudson suggest you say when someone criticises you?
back: "Ouch" or "that hurt".

front: Where must the "ouch" come from?
back: From choice, not from blame.

front: Try, the next time a remark stings: say "ouch" out loud, by choice and without blame.
back: Notice what happens in you, and in the other person.

front: What question does Hudson ask about a no?
back: What happens when I open my heart to it?
extra: Do not treat the no as proof that you are bad.

front: What does "collect rejections" mean?
back: Make rejection the goal.

front: Hudson's story: in one telling, when did galleries say yes to the artist who collected rejections?
back: Once the artist stopped trying to convince them.
extra: The number of rejections varies between tellings, from 25 to 50.

front: Hudson's story (2026 interview): what did he offer his barber?
back: $1,000 or $2,000 to collect 50 rejections in 60 days.

front: Hudson's story: how did the barber's 50 rejections turn out?
back: He got two acceptances. He now sells his paintings for a living.

front: What do you write in the blame list?
back: Who you subtly blame, and for what. Next to each name, how you are aggressive toward them.

front: How do you turn resentment into a want?
back: Find what you wanted and never said. Say it as a request.

text:
Tara Howley's method:
1. {{c1::Be with the anger, hurt and fear}}.
2. {{c2::Get curious about what wounded them}}.
3. {{c3::Find the boundary you need}}.
For a goal you keep dodging, write {{c1::50}} ways to try it. Run them {{c2::in order}}. Tick each as {{c3::a win}} and ask {{c4::what you learned}}.

front: What is the shorter form of the 50-tries list?
back: 15 tries, each with what would make it fun.

front: Try, 5 minutes: pick a goal you keep dodging. Write 15 ways to try it, each with what would make it fun.
back: Notice which try you want to run first.

front: After a setback, does a reframe remove the sadness and fear?
back: No. Feel them first, then go back to the list.

front: What do you say out loud about the criticism or failure you dread?
back: "I can't wait." You say you look forward to it.

front: What question does Hudson ask about perfectionism?
back: Whose standard is it? Is my perfection an effort to please a critical parent?

front: How does "draft twice" work?
back: The first pass is playful and unjudged. Bring the harsh editor only on later passes.

front: What is "applaud mistakes" at a team meeting?
back: Each person names a failure, and the group claps.

front: Try now, 1 minute, eyes closed: you are stuck on an island with your needs met, among people who love you without condition. Who are you after 10 years?
back: Notice that self-attack is not what grows you.

front: What does the island of saints exercise show?
back: That self-attack is not what grows you.

front: You hear "you are enough" and notice your reaction. What do you ask next?
back: What would I lose if I stopped believing I must be more?

front: What journal question does Hudson give for not feeling enough?
back: What would it take to feel enough after I had fixed everything?

front: What does Hudson say eases imposter feelings faster than building more skill?
back: Telling someone a thing you judge yourself for, and seeing how they respond.

front: Which question does Hudson swap in for "how do I protect myself?"
back: "How do I serve here?"

front: What does Hudson say arrogance and self-doubt have in common?
back: They are the same habit: thinking about yourself all the time.

text: You cannot ask how to do this job {{c1::with an open heart}} and ask {{c2::if you are good enough}} at once.

front: In "say what you do not know", what do you tell the group?
back: What you know and what you do not know. Then ask what they know.

front: Each time you judge someone, what does Hudson suggest you do?
back: Ask what emotion you are avoiding, and feel it for 20 seconds.

context: Overwhelm: five minutes every two hours
front: What is the "five minutes every two hours" experiment?
back: Sit and do nothing for 5 minutes every 2 hours. Try it for one day.
extra: You may cry, scream or simply enjoy it.

front: When there is no room to process a feeling, how do you breathe?
back: Slowly, with the in-breath and out-breath equal.

front: What must you not use even breath for?
back: To push the feeling down. Feel it later.

text: Between meetings, shake for {{c1::2 to 3 minutes}}, yawn {{c2::10 to 20 times}}, or cry for {{c3::a minute or two}}.

front: Try now, 2 minutes: stand and let your body shake. Then yawn a few times.
back: Notice whether your head feels clearer for the next task.

text:
1. Notice {{c1::when you run on adrenaline}}.
2. Name {{c2::the trigger}}.
3. Find a way to {{c3::do the task without it}}.

front: How do you list what drains you?
back: For one week, after each task, ask if it gave or took energy.

front: What do you do with each task that drains you?
back: Find a way to enjoy it, or hand it off.

front: When you rest, what comes first?
back: Sleep and food.

front: After sleep and food, what do you ask to choose your rest?
back: Which way you are worn out: emotionally, socially, mentally or sensorily. Then match the rest to it.

front: How can you tell that something was not real rest?
back: You are still drained after it.

front: When rest starts to feel good, what does Hudson suggest?
back: Stay in it. Do not rush back when you start to feel fine.

front: Try, the next time you worry: ask "What am I scared will happen?" Then ask "What would I have to feel if it did?" Feel that for a minute.
back: Notice whether the worry changes once you feel what is under it.

context: Resentment: turn it into a want
front: Try, 2 minutes: pick one person you resent a little. What did you want from them and never say? Write it as a request.
back: Notice how the resentment changes when it becomes a want.
